claim: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is critical for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
source: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is critical for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors, but the underlying neural codes remain poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature establishing RSG's role in these behaviors

claim: The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum strongly and selectively recruit small low-rheobase (LR) pyramidal cells in RSG.
source: The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum, sources of spatial information, strongly and selectively recruit small low-rheobase (LR) pyramidal cells in RSG.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic circuit mapping experiments shown in Figures 1-2 and Figure 5

claim: Regular-spiking (RS) cells are preferentially controlled by claustral and anterior cingulate inputs.
source: In contrast, neighboring regular-spiking (RS) cells are preferentially controlled by claustral and anterior cingulate inputs, sources of mostly non-spatial information.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic circuit mapping shown in Figures 3-4

claim: Precise sublaminar axonal and dendritic arborization within RSG layer 1 permits parallel processing.
source: Precise sublaminar axonal and dendritic arborization within RSG layer 1, in particular, permits this parallel processing.
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and projection density data shown in Figures 2-6

claim: Thalamocortical synaptic dynamics enable computational models of LR neurons to compute the speed of head rotation.
source: Observed thalamocortical synaptic dynamics enable computational models of LR neurons to compute the speed of head rotation, despite receiving head direction inputs that do not explicitly encode speed.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figures 8-10

claim: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with spatial navigation.
source: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors, including spatial navigation, learning, memory, fear conditioning, imagination, and planning for the future (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Chang et al., 2020; Chrastil, 2018; Hinman et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with learning.
source: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors, including spatial navigation, learning, memory, fear conditioning, imagination, and planning for the future (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Chang et al., 2020; Chrastil, 2018; Hinman et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with memory.
source: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors, including spatial navigation, learning, memory, fear conditioning, imagination, and planning for the future (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Chang et al., 2020; Chrastil, 2018; Hinman et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with fear conditioning.
source: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors, including spatial navigation, learning, memory, fear conditioning, imagination, and planning for the future (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Chang et al., 2020; Chrastil, 2018; Hinman et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with imagination.
source: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors, including spatial navigation, learning, memory, fear conditioning, imagination, and planning for the future (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Chang et al., 2020; Chrastil, 2018; Hinman et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with planning for the future.
source: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors, including spatial navigation, learning, memory, fear conditioning, imagination, and planning for the future (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Chang et al., 2020; Chrastil, 2018; Hinman et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: The RSG is among the most densely connected regions of the brain.
source: The RSG is also among the most densely connected regions of the brain, integrating inputs from a bevy of cortical and subcortical sources and serving as part of the default mode network (Greicius et al., 2009; Kaboodvand et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Whitesell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: The RSG serves as part of the default mode network.
source: The RSG is also among the most densely connected regions of the brain, integrating inputs from a bevy of cortical and subcortical sources and serving as part of the default mode network (Greicius et al., 2009; Kaboodvand et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Whitesell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Anatomical connections of the RSG are well-documented.
source: While these anatomical connections are well-documented (Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; van Groen and Wyss, 1990; Whitesell et al., 2021; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992), few studies have examined their functional nature (Nitzan et al., 2020; Yamawaki et al., 2019b; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2016a), and cell-type specificity has yet to be sufficiently explored.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple anatomical studies

claim: Few studies have examined the functional nature of RSG connections.
source: While these anatomical connections are well-documented (Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; van Groen and Wyss, 1990; Whitesell et al., 2021; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992), few studies have examined their functional nature (Nitzan et al., 2020; Yamawaki et al., 2019b; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2016a), and cell-type specificity has yet to be sufficiently explored.
evidence: Supported by citations to limited prior functional studies

claim: Cell-type specificity of RSG connections has yet to be sufficiently explored.
source: While these anatomical connections are well-documented (Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; van Groen and Wyss, 1990; Whitesell et al., 2021; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992), few studies have examined their functional nature (Nitzan et al., 2020; Yamawaki et al., 2019b; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2016a), and cell-type specificity has yet to be sufficiently explored.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: Cortical regions, including the RSG, receive inputs from one or more thalamic nuclei.
source: Cortical regions, including the RSG, receive inputs from one or more thalamic nuclei (Herkenham, 1986; Herkenham, 1980; Jones, 2001; Jones, 1998; Peters, 1979; Van Groen and Wyss, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: Thalamic relay cells are grouped into three distinct classes: core, intralaminar, and paralaminar/ventral midline (matrix) nuclei.
source: Thalamic relay cells (Clascá et al., 2012) are grouped into three distinct classes: core, intralaminar, and paralaminar/ventral midline (matrix) nuclei (Hanbery and Jasper, 1953; Herkenham, 1986; Jones, 2001; Jones, 1998; Morison and Dempsey, 1941; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on thalamic organization

claim: Thalamic matrix nuclei project predominantly to layer 1 of many cortical regions.
source: Thalamic matrix nuclei project predominantly to layer 1 of many cortical regions (Herkenham, 1986; Herkenham, 1980), resulting in subtype-specific activation of cortical inhibitory (Anastasiades et al., 2021; Cruikshank et al., 2012; Delevich et al., 2015) and excitatory neurons (Collins et al., 2018; Cruikshank et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2018; Rodriguez-Moreno et al., 2020; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009; Van der Werf et al., 2002; Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies

claim: Matrix thalamocortical inputs result in subtype-specific activation of cortical inhibitory neurons.
source: Thalamic matrix nuclei project predominantly to layer 1 of many cortical regions (Herkenham, 1986; Herkenham, 1980), resulting in subtype-specific activation of cortical inhibitory (Anastasiades et al., 2021; Cruikshank et al., 2012; Delevich et al., 2015) and excitatory neurons (Collins et al., 2018; Cruikshank et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2018; Rodriguez-Moreno et al., 2020; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009; Van der Werf et al., 2002; Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior functional studies

claim: Matrix thalamocortical inputs result in subtype-specific activation of cortical excitatory neurons.
source: Thalamic matrix nuclei project predominantly to layer 1 of many cortical regions (Herkenham, 1986; Herkenham, 1980), resulting in subtype-specific activation of cortical inhibitory (Anastasiades et al., 2021; Cruikshank et al., 2012; Delevich et al., 2015) and excitatory neurons (Collins et al., 2018; Cruikshank et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2018; Rodriguez-Moreno et al., 2020; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009; Van der Werf et al., 2002; Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior functional studies

claim: Matrix thalamocortical inputs from the anterior thalamus influence layer 5 pyramidal cells in RSG.
source: Matrix thalamocortical (TC) inputs from the anterior thalamus, which contains the highest proportion of head direction cells in the brain (Taube and Bassett, 2003), influence layer 5 pyramidal cells in RSG (Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: The anterior thalamus contains the highest proportion of head direction cells in the brain.
source: Matrix thalamocortical (TC) inputs from the anterior thalamus, which contains the highest proportion of head direction cells in the brain (Taube and Bassett, 2003), influence layer 5 pyramidal cells in RSG (Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Potential subtype-specific responses of RSG neurons to anterior thalamic inputs have yet to be examined.
source: However, potential subtype-specific responses and their functional impact on the encoding of directional information in RSG have yet to be examined.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: The cortex, including the RSG, receives widespread inputs from the densely connected claustrum.
source: The cortex, including the RSG, also receives widespread inputs from the densely connected claustrum (Brown et al., 2017; Crick and Koch, 2005; Goll et al., 2015; Jackson et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2016; Narikiyo et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2017; White and Mathur, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: The claustrum innervates both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: As with TC signaling, the claustrum innervates both excitatory (da Costa et al., 2010; Narikiyo et al., 2020) and inhibitory (Jackson et al., 2018; Narikiyo et al., 2020; Salerno et al., 1984) neurons via precise laminar targeting (Wang et al., 2017) and projects to many of the same cortical regions as the thalamus (Burman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The claustrum projects to many of the same cortical regions as the thalamus.
source: As with TC signaling, the claustrum innervates both excitatory (da Costa et al., 2010; Narikiyo et al., 2020) and inhibitory (Jackson et al., 2018; Narikiyo et al., 2020; Salerno et al., 1984) neurons via precise laminar targeting (Wang et al., 2017) and projects to many of the same cortical regions as the thalamus (Burman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior anatomical study

claim: Claustrocortical projections are thought to regulate complex functions.
source: Claustrocortical (ClaC) projections are thought to regulate complex functions (Crick and Koch, 2005; Goll et al., 2015; Jackson et al., 2018; Kitanishi and Matsuo, 2017; Narikiyo et al., 2020; Renouard et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2012; White and Mathur, 2018), including the coordination and amplification of correlated signals across cortical regions (Kim et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2012; Smythies et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The RSG is one of few regions that does not return reciprocal connections to the claustrum.
source: Surprisingly, the RSG is one of few regions that does not return reciprocal connections to the claustrum (Zingg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior anatomical study

claim: No studies have investigated the functional nature or subtype-specificity of claustrocortical inputs to RSG neurons.
source: Despite the unique unidirectional nature of this connection, no studies have investigated the functional nature or subtype-specificity of ClaC inputs to RSG neurons.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: The RSG receives direct innervation from the secondary motor cortex.
source: The RSG receives direct innervation from the secondary motor cortex (Yamawaki et al., 2016a), contralateral RSG (Sempere-Ferràndez et al., 2018; Wyss et al., 1990), and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; van Groen and Wyss, 1990), among others.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior anatomical study

claim: The RSG receives direct innervation from contralateral RSG.
source: The RSG receives direct innervation from the secondary motor cortex (Yamawaki et al., 2016a), contralateral RSG (Sempere-Ferràndez et al., 2018; Wyss et al., 1990), and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; van Groen and Wyss, 1990), among others.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: The RSG receives direct innervation from anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
source: The RSG receives direct innervation from the secondary motor cortex (Yamawaki et al., 2016a), contralateral RSG (Sempere-Ferràndez et al., 2018; Wyss et al., 1990), and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; van Groen and Wyss, 1990), among others.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: The RSG and ACC have been implicated in several shared limbic and cognitive functions, including fear conditioning.
source: The RSG and ACC, in particular, have been implicated in several shared limbic and cognitive functions, including fear conditioning (Frankland et al., 2004; Han et al., 2003; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b), but the cellular targets of ACC inputs to RSG have not been identified.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior functional studies

claim: The cellular targets of ACC inputs to RSG have not been identified.
source: The RSG and ACC, in particular, have been implicated in several shared limbic and cognitive functions, including fear conditioning (Frankland et al., 2004; Han et al., 2003; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b), but the cellular targets of ACC inputs to RSG have not been identified.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: The superficial layers of RSG contain two subtypes of principal excitatory pyramidal neurons: the low-rheobase (LR) neuron and the regular-spiking (RS) neuron.
source: Within the RSG, the superficial layers contain two subtypes of principal excitatory pyramidal neurons that have strikingly distinct physiology, morphology, and computational capabilities: the low-rheobase (LR) neuron and the regular-spiking (RS) neuron (Brennan et al., 2020; Kurotani et al., 2013; Yousuf et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: LR and RS neurons have strikingly distinct physiology, morphology, and computational capabilities.
source: Within the RSG, the superficial layers contain two subtypes of principal excitatory pyramidal neurons that have strikingly distinct physiology, morphology, and computational capabilities: the low-rheobase (LR) neuron and the regular-spiking (RS) neuron (Brennan et al., 2020; Kurotani et al., 2013; Yousuf et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: LR neurons are distinguished from RS neurons by their unique intrinsic properties, predominantly the low rheobase, high input resistance, lack of adaptation, and narrow spike width.
source: Using whole-cell patch clamp recordings, we again distinguished LR from RS neurons by their unique intrinsic properties, predominantly the low rheobase, high input resistance, lack of adaptation, and narrow spike width (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1 - Table 1, and Supplementary file 1 - Table 2; Brennan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary tables

claim: Virus injections into the anterodorsal and anteroventral thalamic nuclei resulted in ChR2-eYFP expression in thalamocortical axons and terminals predominantly in layer 1a and in layer 3 of superficial RSG.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Odagiri et al., 2011; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; van Groen and Wyss, 1990; Yamawaki et al., 2019b), virus injections into the anterodorsal and anteroventral thalamic nuclei (ADAV) resulted in ChR2-eYFP expression in thalamocortical (TC) axons and terminals predominantly in layer 1a (L1a; the most superficial part of layer 1) and in layer 3 (L3) of superficial RSG (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citations to prior studies

claim: LR neurons were strongly driven past spike threshold by thalamic inputs while RS neurons exhibited far smaller EPSPs.
source: From resting membrane potentials of approximately −65 mV, LR neurons were strongly driven past spike threshold by these thalamic inputs while RS neurons exhibited far smaller EPSPs (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Thalamic stimulation evoked a significant increase in spiking in LR neurons but not RS neurons.
source: Compared to their baseline activity, this stimulation evoked a significant increase in spiking in LR neurons (p=0.002, Wilcoxon rank sum test) but not RS neurons (p=0.19, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1G

claim: LR neurons had a significantly larger increase in spike rate evoked by optical pulse than RS neurons.
source: The LR neurons thus had a significantly larger increase in spike rate evoked by the optical pulse than RS neurons (p=0.0012, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1H

claim: LR neurons receive stronger activation from thalamocortical inputs than their neighboring L3 RS neurons.
source: This suggests that LR neurons receive stronger activation from TC inputs than their neighboring L3 RS neurons.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential responses to TC stimulation

claim: Apical dendrites of LR neurons were most densely localized to L1a, with basal dendrites remaining confined to L3.
source: Apical dendrites of LR neurons were most densely localized to L1a, with basal dendrites remaining confined to L3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 2C

claim: RS apical dendrites rarely entered L1a, instead existing in the deeper subdivisions of layer 1 (L1b/c), with basal dendrites primarily in upper layer 5.
source: In contrast, RS apical dendrites rarely entered L1a, instead existing in the deeper subdivisions of layer 1 (L1b/c), with basal dendrites primarily in upper layer 5 (L5; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 2D

claim: ADAV axons and terminal arbors are localized in L1a and weakly in L3.
source: Projection density analysis showed localization of ADAV axons and terminal arbors in L1a and weakly in L3 (Figure 2C&D).
evidence: Supported by projection density analysis shown in Figure 2C and 2D

claim: Dendrites of LR, but not RS, cells selectively co-localize within layers 1a and 3 with ADAV thalamocortical afferents.
source: Thus, dendrites of LR, but not RS, cells selectively co-localize within layers 1a and 3 with ADAV TC afferents (Figure 2C&D).
evidence: Supported by morphological and projection density data shown in Figure 2C and 2D

claim: The anterior thalamic-retrosplenial circuit at least partially obeys Peters' rule.
source: This anatomical colocalization of LR, but not RS, dendrites with TC axons coupled with the increase in LR, but not RS, spiking in response to TC optical stimulation indicates that the anterior thalamic-retrosplenial circuit at least partially obeys Peters' rule, which states that neuronal populations with anatomically overlapping axonal and dendritic arbors are more likely to show functional connectivity Peters, 1979; Peters and Feldman, 1976.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical and functional data, with reference to Peters' rule

claim: LR neurons had a significantly larger EPSP amplitude in response to L1a LED stimulation compared to RS cell responses.
source: When delivering 1 ms high LED power light pulses, we indeed found that LR neurons had a significantly larger excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) amplitude in response to the L1a LED stimulation compared to RS cell responses (p=0.0185, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: LR cells showed significantly larger EPSP amplitudes compared to L5 RS neurons in response to layer one stimulation.
source: Notably, in response to layer one stimulation, LR cells also showed significantly larger EPSP amplitudes compared to L5 RS neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which have been previously shown to respond to TC input (Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior study

claim: LR neurons, rather than layer 3 or 5 RS neurons, are the predominant RSG cell type receiving and processing head direction inputs from the anterior thalamus.
source: This suggests that LR neurons, rather than layer 3 or 5 RS neurons, are the predominant RSG cell type receiving and processing head direction inputs from the anterior thalamus.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential responses to TC input

claim: LR neurons have the largest EPSP amplitude when the LED pulse is targeting layer 1a, corresponding with the peak projection density of ADAV axons and terminal arbors at this lamina.
source: We found that LR neurons have the largest EPSP amplitude when the LED pulse is targeting layer 1a, corresponding with the peak projection density of ADAV axons and terminal arbors at this lamina.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from high-resolution optogenetic stimulation protocol

claim: RS neurons showed much smaller EPSP amplitude with no significant variation in response across the layers.
source: In contrast, the RS neuron showed much smaller EPSP amplitude with no significant variation in response across the layers (Figure 2F&G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and 2G

claim: Within the LR cell population, LR cells have significantly larger responses at L1a and cell body compared to L1/2.
source: We found that within the LR cell population, LR cells have significantly larger responses at L1a (p=0.00001) and cell body (p=0.0006) compared to L1/2 (paired t-test; Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: The lamination of functional responses in the LR population precisely aligns with the lamination of ADAV axons and terminal arbors within superficial layers.
source: This lamination of functional responses in the LR population precisely aligns with the lamination of ADAV axons and terminal arbors within these superficial layers.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of functional responses and anatomical projection patterns

claim: RS EPSP amplitudes at layers 1a, cell body, L5sup, and L5dp did not differ from responses at L1/2.
source: In contrast, RS EPSP amplitudes at layers 1a, cell body, L5sup, and L5dp did not differ from responses at L1/2 (p>0.05 for all; paired t-test), indicating that there is no significant lamination of functional responses to thalamic inputs in the RS population, likely due to their relative lack of response to these inputs in general (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: The connectivity between anterior thalamic TC arbors and L3 principal neurons in RSG depends on the precise sublaminar colocalization of both local principal cells' dendrites and incoming thalamocortical axons.
source: Thus, the connectivity between anterior thalamic TC arbors and L3 principal neurons in RSG highlights a circuit that depends on the precise sublaminar colocalization of both local principal cells' dendrites and incoming thalamocortical axons.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical and functional data

claim: LR neurons are uniquely anatomically adapted to respond to incoming inputs from the anterior thalamus due to a precise overlap of their apical dendrites with the dense thalamic axons and terminals in the uppermost sublamina of L1 (L1a).
source: This demonstrates that LR neurons are uniquely anatomically adapted to respond to incoming inputs from the anterior thalamus, where ~ 60% of neurons are head direction cells (Taube, 1995; Taube and Bassett, 2003), due to a precise overlap of their apical dendrites with the dense thalamic axons and terminals in the uppermost sublamina of L1 (L1a).
evidence: Inferred from anatomical and functional data, with citation to prior study on HD cells

claim: Approximately 60% of neurons in the anterior thalamus are head direction cells.
source: This demonstrates that LR neurons are uniquely anatomically adapted to respond to incoming inputs from the anterior thalamus, where ~ 60% of neurons are head direction cells (Taube, 1995; Taube and Bassett, 2003), due to a precise overlap of their apical dendrites with the dense thalamic axons and terminals in the uppermost sublamina of L1 (L1a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Claustrocortical and ACC corticocortical projections exhibit distinct laminar organization within target cortical layers.
source: Both claustrocortical (ClaC) and ACC corticocortical (CC) projections have been anatomically shown to exhibit distinct laminar organization within its target cortical layers (Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; Vogt and Miller, 1983; Wang et al., 2017), but the precise functional targets of claustral and cingulate inputs to superficial RSG have, to our knowledge, never been examined.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: The precise functional targets of claustral and cingulate inputs to superficial RSG have never been examined.
source: Both claustrocortical (ClaC) and ACC corticocortical (CC) projections have been anatomically shown to exhibit distinct laminar organization within its target cortical layers (Van Groen and Wyss, 2003; Vogt and Miller, 1983; Wang et al., 2017), but the precise functional targets of claustral and cingulate inputs to superficial RSG have, to our knowledge, never been examined.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: ChR2 injections into CLA resulted in expression of CLA axons and terminals in layers 1c, 2, and 5.
source: ChR2 injections into CLA (Figure 3A) resulted in expression of CLA axons and terminals in layers 1 c, 2, and 5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: CLA expression pattern is distinct from the thalamic expression localized to layers 1a and 3.
source: This expression pattern is distinct from the thalamic expression localized to layers 1a and 3 (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: RS, but not LR, apical dendrites anatomically overlap with CLA arbors in superficial layers 1c and two and upper layer 5.
source: Dendritic lamination plots of LR and RS dendrites and projection density plots of CLA axons and terminal arbors show that RS, but not LR, apical dendrites anatomically overlap with CLA arbors in superficial layers 1 c and two and upper layer 5 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by morphological and projection density data shown in Figure 3D

claim: RS neurons have significantly larger responses to CLA input compared to LR neurons when stimulated at layer 1/2.
source: Using the same targeted optogenetic stimulation approach as previously described (see Materials and methods), we found that RS neurons have significantly larger responses to CLA input compared to LR neurons when stimulated at layer 1/2 (p=0.0000035, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 3E), the area of the strongest superficial projection density of CLA arbors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: Layer 5 RS neurons exhibited significantly larger EPSP amplitudes in response to CLA inputs compared to LR cells.
source: Similarly, layer 5 RS neurons exhibited significantly larger EPSP amplitudes in response to CLA inputs compared to LR cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: RS neurons in both RSG L3 and L5 are the primary recipients of CLA inputs.
source: This again indicates that while LR neurons may be optimally positioned to receive thalamic input, RS neurons in both RSG L3 and L5 are instead the primary recipients of CLA inputs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential responses to CLA input

claim: RS neurons have the largest EPSP amplitude when the LED pulse is stimulating both layer 1c and 5sup and weakest EPSP amplitude at layer 1a, corresponding with the strongest and weakest projection density of CLA afferents at these laminar locations.
source: We found that RS neurons have the largest EPSP amplitude when the LED pulse is stimulating both layer 1c and 5sup and weakest EPSP amplitude at layer 1a, corresponding with, respectively, the strongest and the weakest projection density of CLA afferents at these laminar locations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from high-resolution optogenetic stimulation protocol

claim: Within the RS cell population, RS cells have significantly larger responses at L1/2 and L5sup compared to those at L1a.
source: Population analysis showed that within the RS cell population, RS cells have significantly larger responses at L1/2 (p=0.00725) and L5sup (p=0.0301) compared to those at L1a (paired t-test; Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G

claim: The lamination of functional responses in the RS cell precisely aligns with the lamination of ClaC axons and terminal arbors within these layers.
source: This lamination of functional responses in the RS cell precisely aligns with the lamination of ClaC axons and terminal arbors within these layers.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of functional responses and anatomical projection patterns

claim: LR EPSP amplitudes across all layers were much lower in magnitude and did not differ from responses at L1a, indicating no significant lamination of functional responses to ClaC inputs in the LR population.
source: In contrast, LR EPSP amplitudes across all layers were much lower in magnitude and did not differ from responses at L1a (p>0.05 for all; paired t-test; Figure 3G), indicating no significant lamination of functional responses to ClaC inputs in the LR population.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G

claim: Corticocortical inputs from the anterior cingulate target L1b/c and, to a lesser extent, L5.
source: Using the same CRACM approach to examine ACC inputs to RSG (Figure 4A), we found that corticocortical inputs from the anterior cingulate target L1b/c and, to a lesser extent, L5 (Figure 4B), partially resembling the laminar pattern seen with CLA arbors (Figure 3B) and overlapping precisely with RS, but not LR, dendrites (Figure 3C&D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: When stimulating ACC arbors at L1/2, RS cells had significantly larger EPSP amplitudes compared to LR cells.
source: Indeed, when stimulating ACC arbors at L1/2, RS cells had significantly larger EPSP amplitudes compared to LR cells (p=0.0019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: RS cells have the largest EPSP response to ACC inputs at L1/2, while the same minimum LED stimulation power elicits no response in layer 1a.
source: When examining the lamination of these inputs with higher spatial resolution, we found that RS cells have the largest EPSP response to ACC inputs at L1/2, while the same minimum LED stimulation power elicits no response in layer 1a (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Population analysis of RS cells revealed significantly larger responses to optogenetic stimulation of ACC inputs at the L1/2 and cell body compared to L1a stimulation.
source: Population analysis of RS cells revealed significantly larger responses to optogenetic stimulation of ACC inputs at the L1/2 (p=0.000037) and cell body (p=0.000525) compared to L1a stimulation (Figure 4G), reflecting the precise overlap of ACC arbors and RS dendrites.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: Both claustrocortical and corticocortical inputs to RSG target RS apical dendrites at the lower divisions of L1, whereas thalamocortical inputs preferentially target the apical dendrites of LR cells in upper L1.
source: Thus, both claustrocortical and corticocortical inputs to RSG target RS apical dendrites at the lower divisions of L1 (L1c and L1b/c, respectively), whereas thalamocortical inputs preferentially target the apical dendrites of LR cells in upper L1 (L1a).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential laminar targeting

claim: Parallel circuits in RSG process TC versus ClaC and CC information, and this parallel processing is enabled by precise sublaminar organization of afferent axons and layer three principal cell apical dendrites.
source: This again indicates that parallel circuits in RSG process TC versus ClaC and CC information, and this parallel processing is enabled by precise sublaminar organization of afferent axons and layer three principal cell apical dendrites.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential targeting of LR versus RS cells

claim: Dorsal subiculum serves to transmit allocentric spatial information such as axis cell and boundary vector signals.
source: Previous work has shown that dorsal subiculum (DS), which serves to transmit allocentric spatial information such as axis cell and boundary vector signals (Lever et al., 2009; Derdikman, 2009; Olson et al., 2017; Simonnet and Brecht, 2019; Bicanski and Burgess, 2020), also precisely targets layer 2/3 principal neurons in RSG (Nitzan et al., 2020; Yamawaki et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Dorsal subiculum precisely targets layer 2/3 principal neurons in RSG.
source: Previous work has shown that dorsal subiculum (DS), which serves to transmit allocentric spatial information such as axis cell and boundary vector signals (Lever et al., 2009; Derdikman, 2009; Olson et al., 2017; Simonnet and Brecht, 2019; Bicanski and Burgess, 2020), also precisely targets layer 2/3 principal neurons in RSG (Nitzan et al., 2020; Yamawaki et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: DS inputs overlap with LR cell bodies and basal dendrites and have been shown to evoke larger excitatory postsynaptic currents in superficial compared to layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: These inputs overlap with LR cell bodies and basal dendrites and have been shown to evoke larger excitatory postsynaptic currents in superficial compared to layer 5 pyramidal neurons (Nitzan et al., 2020; Yamawaki et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: DS afferents to layer 3 of RSG precisely overlap with LR basal and, to a lesser degree, proximal apical dendrites but not RS basal dendrites.
source: We found that DS afferents to layer 3 of RSG precisely overlap with LR basal and, to a lesser degree, proximal apical dendrites (Figure 5C) but not RS basal dendrites (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by morphological and projection density data shown in Figure 5C and 5D

claim: LR neurons responded with significantly larger EPSPs compared to RS neurons when DS inputs were stimulated at the cell body in layer 3.
source: Correspondingly, LR neurons responded with significantly larger EPSPs compared to RS neurons when DS inputs were stimulated at the cell body in layer 3 (p=0.004; Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E

claim: LR cells had significantly larger responses at layers 1/2 and 3 compared to L1a in response to DS input.
source: Our high-resolution protocol and population analysis also confirmed that LR cells had significantly larger responses at layers 1/2 and 3 compared to L1a (L1/2 p=0.0132, L3 p=0.0135; Figure 5F&G), suggesting the possibility of integration of synchronous anterior thalamic and dorsal subicular inputs by LR neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F and 5G

claim: RS cells showed no significant laminal differences in response to DS input.
source: In contrast, RS cells showed no significant laminal differences in response to DS input (p>0.05 for all; Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5G

claim: Inputs from both the dorsal subiculum and anterior thalamus target LR cells, reflecting their precise overlap with LR dendrites, while the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex instead target RS cells.
source: Thus, inputs from both the dorsal subiculum and anterior thalamus target LR cells, reflecting their precise overlap with LR dendrites, while the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex instead target RS cells.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential targeting patterns

claim: LR dendrites are strongly and significantly positively correlated with both ADAV and DS axons.
source: We found that LR dendrites are strongly and significantly positively correlated with both ADAV (r = 0.88, p<0.001) and DS (r = 0.69, p=1.41e-254) axons.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of morphological data

claim: RS dendrites are strongly correlated with CLA and ACC axons.
source: In contrast, RS dendrites are strongly correlated with CLA (r = 0.29, p=4.82e-36) and ACC (r = 0.43, p=5.73e-82) axons.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of morphological data

claim: LR dendrites are significantly negatively correlated with both CLA and ACC axons.
source: Notably, LR dendrites are significantly negatively correlated with both CLA (r = −0.49, p=1.16e-110) and ACC (r = −0.15, p=1.00e-10) axons, and RS dendrites are negatively correlated with ADAV (r = −0.55, p=2.47e-145) and DS (r = −0.44, p=7.74e-85) axons (Figure 6B&C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B and 6C

claim: RS dendrites are negatively correlated with ADAV and DS axons.
source: Notably, LR dendrites are significantly negatively correlated with both CLA (r = −0.49, p=1.16e-110) and ACC (r = −0.15, p=1.00e-10) axons, and RS dendrites are negatively correlated with ADAV (r = −0.55, p=2.47e-145) and DS (r = −0.44, p=7.74e-85) axons (Figure 6B&C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B and 6C

claim: ADAV and DS inputs to RSG, which both at least in part target layer 3, were significantly positively correlated with one another.
source: We also compared laminar expression of afferents from the four input regions and found that ADAV and DS inputs to RSG, which both at least in part target layer 3, were significantly positively correlated with one another (r = 0.55, p=2.93e-143).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of projection density data

claim: CLA and ACC inputs, which both target the lower divisions of L1 as well as L5, were also significantly positively correlated.
source: Similarly, CLA and ACC inputs, which both target the lower divisions of L1 as well as L5, were also significantly positively correlated (r = 0.23, p=2.3e-23).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of projection density data

claim: ADAV and DS inputs were significantly negatively correlated with both CLA and ACC inputs.
source: However, ADAV and DS inputs were significantly negatively correlated with both CLA and ACC inputs, confirming that these two streams target separate sublayers within RSG (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B and 6C

claim: Dendrite-dendrite correlations of LR and RS cell populations were strongly anti-correlated.
source: Dendrite-dendrite correlations of LR and RS cell populations were also strongly anti-correlated (r = −0.65, p=3.00e-215; Figure 6C), highlighting the distinct anatomical organization of these two neighboring principal cell types.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Precise, fine-grained laminar organization of LR and RS dendrites and afferent axons creates a parallel circuit in which LR neurons are selectively optimized to integrate incoming spatial information.
source: Taken together, these axon-axon, dendrite-dendrite, and axon-dendrite correlations indicate that precise, fine-grained laminar organization of LR and RS dendrites and afferent axons creates a parallel circuit in which LR neurons are selectively optimized to integrate incoming spatial information (Figure 6D).
evidence: Inferred from correlation analyses and experimental data

claim: Contralateral RSG inputs to RSG showed lamination and resulting cell-type-specific targeting resembling that of projections from CLA and ACC.
source: Supplemental examination of contralateral RSG (cRSG) inputs to RSG showed lamination and resulting cell-type-specific targeting resembling that of projections from CLA and ACC (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Contralateral RSG inputs targeted L1c, L2, and L5, resulting in strong activation of RS cells, with almost no responses in LR cells.
source: Specifically, cRSG inputs targeted L1c, L2, and L5, resulting in strong activation of RS cells, with almost no responses in LR cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Inputs from CLA, ACC and cRSG follow a structured pattern by which these inputs preferentially control RS cells, while ADAV and DS projections target LR cells.
source: This again suggests that inputs from CLA, ACC and cRSG follow a structured pattern by which these inputs preferentially control RS cells, while ADAV and DS projections target LR cells.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing consistent targeting patterns

claim: Laminar dichotomies similar to those seen in RSG also exist between TC and ClaC/corticocortical projections to other cortical regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Importantly, laminar dichotomies similar to those seen here in RSG also exist between TC and ClaC/corticocortical projections to other cortical regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex (Cruikshank et al., 2012), as also revealed by our examination of anatomical datasets from the Allen Brain Institute (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study and examination of Allen Brain Institute data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: The findings may highlight a more universal framework by which other cortical regions integrate and process thalamic versus claustral and cortical inputs.
source: Thus, our findings may also highlight a more universal framework by which other cortical regions integrate and process thalamic versus claustral and cortical inputs.
evidence: Speculative inference based on comparison with other cortical regions

claim: 10 Hz anterior thalamic inputs from ADAV to RSG LR neurons were uniquely and significantly depressing.
source: In contrast to previously documented thalamocortical matrix inputs to both superficial pyramidal cells and interneurons (Anastasiades et al., 2021; Cruikshank et al., 2012), 10 Hz anterior thalamic inputs from ADAV to RSG LR neurons were uniquely and significantly depressing (p=1.02e-5, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 7A&B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A and 7B, with citation to prior studies for comparison

claim: 10 Hz DS inputs to LR neurons were not depressing and exhibited weak facilitation.
source: In contrast, 10 Hz DS inputs to LR neurons were not depressing and exhibited weak facilitation (Figure 7A&B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and 7B

claim: Both CLA and ACC inputs to RS cells were weakly facilitating.
source: Both CLA and ACC inputs to RS cells were also weakly facilitating (Figure 7C&D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and 7D

claim: The synaptic depression of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons is unique among the inputs examined and also distinct from anterior thalamic inputs to superficial principal neurons in PFC and ACC.
source: Thus, the synaptic depression of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons is unique among the inputs examined here and also distinct from anterior thalamic inputs to superficial principal neurons in PFC and ACC (Cruikshank et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data with citation to prior study for comparison

claim: ADAV inputs to LR cells do not show synaptic depression at the much slower stimulation frequency of 0.1 Hz.
source: As expected, we found that ADAV inputs to LR cells do not show synaptic depression at the much slower stimulation frequency of 0.1 Hz (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 panel C), but 40 Hz inputs resulted in stronger depression than 10 Hz (p=0.0022, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1 panel B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: 40 Hz ADAV inputs resulted in stronger depression than 10 Hz.
source: As expected, we found that ADAV inputs to LR cells do not show synaptic depression at the much slower stimulation frequency of 0.1 Hz (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 panel C), but 40 Hz inputs resulted in stronger depression than 10 Hz (p=0.0022, Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1 panel B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The firing rate of the postsynaptic LR cell receiving HD input via depressing synapses was strongly correlated with angular head speed.
source: We found that the firing rate of the postsynaptic LR cell receiving HD input via depressing synapses was strongly correlated with angular head speed, giving rise to symmetrical angular head velocity tuning (Figure 8B&C).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8B and 8C

claim: Identical HD inputs transmitted via non-depressing synapses resulted in LR firing rates that were uncorrelated with angular head speed.
source: Identical HD inputs transmitted via non-depressing synapses resulted in LR firing rates that were uncorrelated with angular head speed (Figure 8B,E–F).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8B, 8E, and 8F

claim: In the model, firing rates of input HD cells were not explicitly modulated by angular head velocity; therefore, the observed speed tuning resulted strictly from the depressing synaptic dynamics.
source: It is important to note that in our model, firing rates of input HD cells were not explicitly modulated by angular head velocity; therefore, the observed speed tuning resulted strictly from the depressing synaptic dynamics.
evidence: Based on the design of the computational model

claim: LR cell firing rate was optimally correlated with head speed 24 ms in the past, confirmed by both cross-correlation and mutual information analyses.
source: For the parameter set whose results are depicted, LR cell firing rate was optimally correlated with head speed 24 ms in the past, confirmed by both cross-correlation and mutual information analyses (Figure 8E&F).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8E and 8F

claim: Synaptic depression of HD ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the LR population, producing neurons that are more responsive during faster head turns.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that synaptic depression of HD ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the LR population, producing neurons that are more responsive during faster head turns, and potentially supporting the spatial orientation encoding functions attributed to the RSG (Epstein, 2008; Ino et al., 2007; Milczarek et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from computational modeling results with citations to prior studies on RSG function

claim: Anterior thalamic HD cells display anticipatory firing.
source: Anterior thalamic HD cells display anticipatory firing (Blair et al., 1997), a phenomenon where an HD cell becomes most active at a fixed time interval before the animal is facing that cell's preferred direction (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: In anterior thalamus, the mean anticipatory time interval (ATI) has been reported as 25–50 ms.
source: In anterior thalamus, the mean ATI has been reported as 25–50 ms (Taube, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Increasing ATI from 0 ms to higher values improved the lag between LR firing rate and angular head speed, with larger ATIs resulting in shorter latency between the head movement and LR coding of that angular head speed.
source: Increasing ATI from 0 ms (no anticipation by the HD cell) to higher values (HD cell firing prior to facing the preferred HD) improved the lag between LR firing rate and angular head speed, with larger ATIs resulting in shorter latency between the head movement and LR coding of that angular head speed (Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9C

claim: Larger ATIs improved the angular head speed tuning of LR neurons independent of lag.
source: Remarkably, larger ATIs also improved the angular head speed tuning of LR neurons independent of lag, as quantified by the maximum value (over the full range of lags) of cross-correlation or cross-mutual information (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 9B

claim: Anticipatory firing of HD cells may constitute a powerful coding principle in the thalamo-retrosplenial circuit, helping LR cells to not only encode the current head speed with minimal lag, but also better encode the head speed independent of the lag.
source: Thus, anticipatory firing of HD cells may constitute a powerful coding principle in the thalamo-retrosplenial circuit, helping LR cells to not only encode the current head speed with minimal lag, but also better encode the head speed independent of the lag.
evidence: Inferred from computational modeling results

claim: Analytical analysis showed that LR activity should encode head speed with depressing synapses from simplified HD cells.
source: Our analysis allowed us to mathematically derive that LR activity should encode head speed with depressing synapses from simplified HD cells (see Appendix).
evidence: Supported by analytical mathematical derivation in the Appendix

claim: Anticipatory firing compensates for the lag introduced by integration time, leading to a theoretical parameter regime for which postsynaptic speed coding can be essentially perfect.
source: Moreover, the analysis showed that anticipatory firing compensates for the lag introduced by integration time, leading to a theoretical parameter regime for which postsynaptic speed coding can be essentially perfect (where LR firing rate reflects head speed exactly with minimal latency).
evidence: Supported by analytical mathematical analysis

claim: Postsynaptic activity, at least at lower rotational speeds, is proportional to the square of head speed.
source: Finally, our analysis showed that postsynaptic activity, at least at lower rotational speeds, is proportional to the square of head speed, thereby explaining the concave-up, parabolic shape of the speed-firing rate curve (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analytical mathematical analysis and computational modeling results shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2

claim: Single cell activity in the LR population could encode both head direction and head speed, but there was a clear tradeoff between the two types of information.
source: We found that single cell activity in the LR population could encode both head direction and head speed (Figure 10Aii,Bii,Cii), but there was a clear tradeoff between the two types of information.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 10

claim: The tradeoff between directional versus speed encoding was explained by the level of heterogeneity in the presynaptic preferred direction distribution.
source: This tradeoff between directional versus speed encoding was explained by the level of heterogeneity in the presynaptic preferred direction distribution (Figure 10D–F), making intuitive sense.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 10D-F

claim: Non-uniform HD inputs via depressing thalamocortical synapses represent a simple mechanism by which LR cells can conjunctively encode both head direction and head speed.
source: Thus, non-uniform HD inputs via depressing thalamocortical synapses represent a simple mechanism by which LR cells can conjunctively encode both head direction and head speed.
evidence: Inferred from computational modeling results

claim: LR neurons do not synapse onto neighboring excitatory neurons within layers 2/3.
source: LR neurons do not synapse onto neighboring excitatory neurons within layers 2/3 (Brennan et al., 2020), and no (0/9) pairs tested in this study between LR and layer 5 RS cells exhibited connectivity (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study and experimental data from this study

claim: LR cells likely do not provide any substantial input to other LR cells or any RS cells located in layers 2–5 of ipsilateral RSG.
source: Thus, LR cells likely do not provide any substantial input to other LR cells or any RS cells located in layers 2–5 of ipsilateral RSG.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing lack of connectivity

claim: LR neurons send their axons into the corpus callosum and may likely target homotopic regions of contralateral RSG.
source: Instead, LR neurons send their axons into the corpus callosum and may likely target homotopic regions of contralateral RSG (Brennan et al., 2020; Kurotani et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Retrograde injections into one RSG hemisphere have been shown to predominantly label small contralateral L2/3 cells, most likely corresponding to the LR cells.
source: Indeed, retrograde injections into one RSG hemisphere have been shown to predominantly label small contralateral L2/3 cells (Sripanidkulchai and Wyss, 1987; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003), most likely corresponding to the LR cells that constitute the majority of cells in L2/3 (Brennan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: LR cells constitute the majority of cells in L2/3 of RSG.
source: Indeed, retrograde injections into one RSG hemisphere have been shown to predominantly label small contralateral L2/3 cells (Sripanidkulchai and Wyss, 1987; Van Groen and Wyss, 2003), most likely corresponding to the LR cells that constitute the majority of cells in L2/3 (Brennan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: The small, excitable LR cells are unique among pyramidal cells in RSG, and there is no evidence for such cells in any other cortical regions.
source: The small, excitable LR cells are unique among pyramidal cells in RSG, and there is no evidence, to our knowledge, for such cells in any other cortical regions (Brennan et al., 2020; Holmgren et al., 2003; Jiang et al., 2015; Kurotani et al., 2013; Wyss et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The 'granular' in granular retrosplenial cortex refers to the appearance of dense small cell bodies in superficial RSG.
source: Indeed, the 'granular' in granular retrosplenial cortex refers to the appearance of these dense small cell bodies in superficial RSG (Sripanidkulchai and Wyss, 1987; Vogt and Peters, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: LR cells are the defining morphological feature of RSG.
source: Thus, LR cells are the defining morphological feature of RSG.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that LR cells are the basis for the 'granular' appearance

claim: The low rheobase and lack of spike frequency adaptation of LR neurons are their defining computational features.
source: We have previously reported that the low rheobase and lack of spike frequency adaptation of these neurons are their defining computational features (Brennan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Many other neurons in superficial RSG are also late spiking, including L2/3 fast-spiking (FS) interneurons and some RS neurons.
source: First, many other neurons in superficial RSG are also late spiking (Brennan et al., 2020), with L2/3 fast-spiking (FS) interneurons and also some RS neurons exhibiting a substantial delay to first spike, likely due to increased Kv1.1 or 1.2 channel expression in this region compared to other cortical areas (Kurotani et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Late-spiking is neither a distinctive feature of LR neurons nor excitatory neurons in RSG.
source: Thus, late-spiking is neither a distinctive feature of LR neurons nor excitatory neurons in this region.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that multiple cell types show late-spiking

claim: The name 'late-spiking (LS) neuron' is already the accepted and widely used nomenclature referring to neurogliaform cells.
source: Second, the name 'late-spiking (LS) neuron' is already the accepted and widely used nomenclature referring to a distinct inhibitory neuronal subtype, the neurogliaform cells that are located throughout the cortical layers in many regions of the brain, including within layer 1 of RSG (Cruikshank et al., 2012; Hestrin and Armstrong, 1996; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on neurogliaform cells

claim: Previous work has reported TC-evoked responses in layer 5 RS neurons at their apical dendrites, with some variation in the magnitude of responses across cells.
source: Previous work has reported TC-evoked responses in layer 5 RS neurons at their apical dendrites (Yamawaki et al., 2019b), with some variation in the magnitude of responses across cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Layer 5 is not a homogenous layer, often divided into sublayers 5A and 5B.
source: Layer 5 is not a homogenous layer, often divided into sublayers 5A and 5B (Sempere-Ferràndez et al., 2019; Sempere-Ferràndez et al., 2018; Sigwald et al., 2020; Sripanidkulchai and Wyss, 1987; Yamawaki et al., 2016a) and contains a variety of pyramidal cells, including the thin-tufted and thick-tufted neurons who have been shown to exhibit different responses to external inputs (Sempere-Ferràndez et al., 2018; Wyss et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies

claim: LR cells are the predominant spatial information-encoding subtype within RSG.
source: Further work is needed to determine whether any particular subtype of layer five pyramidal neurons may exhibit substantial TC-evoked responses, but our results, reporting significantly larger responses to TC input by LR neurons, suggest LR cells are the predominant spatial information-encoding subtype within RSG.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing larger TC responses in LR cells

claim: The distinct morphology and intrinsic properties of LR neurons make them ideally suited to integrate head direction input from the thalamus and spatial inputs from the hippocampal formation via the dorsal subiculum.
source: Thus, the distinct morphology and intrinsic properties of LR neurons make them ideally suited to integrate head direction input from the thalamus and spatial inputs from the hippocampal formation via the dorsal subiculum.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing LR responses to both ADAV and DS inputs

claim: Integration of various types of directional and distance information is often stated as the key computational function of the retrosplenial cortex as a whole.
source: Indeed, this integration of various types of directional and distance information is often stated as the key computational function of the retrosplenial cortex as a whole (van Wijngaarden et al., 2020; Burgess et al., 2001; Byrne et al., 2007; Epstein, 2008; Ichinohe et al., 2003; Maguire, 2001), further highlighting the defining role that LR cells are likely to serve in the RSG.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on RSG function

claim: Matrix TC inputs evoke feedforward inhibition to regulate cortical signaling through both disinhibition and the disynaptic inhibition of pyramidal neurons.
source: Matrix TC inputs evoke feedforward inhibition to regulate cortical signaling through both disinhibition (Anastasiades et al., 2021; Delevich et al., 2015) and the disynaptic inhibition of pyramidal neurons (Cruikshank et al., 2012; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: ClaC inputs invoke feedforward inhibition in several cortical regions, particularly through recruitment of neuropeptide Y (NPY) and, to a lesser degree, FS cells.
source: Similarly, ClaC inputs invoke feedforward inhibition in several cortical regions, particularly through recruitment of neuropeptide Y (NPY) and, to a lesser degree, FS cells (Jackson et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Long-range inhibitory signals from CA1 of the hippocampus target apical dendrites in retrosplenial layer 1a, converging with excitatory anterior thalamic inputs, to precisely regulate these TC inputs and establish a hippocampo-thalamo-retrosplenial network.
source: Long-range inhibitory signals from CA1 of the hippocampus also target apical dendrites in retrosplenial layer 1a, converging with excitatory anterior thalamic inputs, to precisely regulate these TC inputs and establish a hippocampo-thalamo-retrosplenial network (Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: The fine-grained laminar overlap of inhibitory signals from CA1 with TC inputs strongly suggests that these inhibitory signals may regulate responses to matrix TC input more strongly for LR than layer 5 RS cells.
source: This fine-grained laminar overlap strongly suggests that these inhibitory signals may regulate responses to matrix TC input more strongly for LR than layer 5 RS cells and should be investigated further, particularly in the context of integration of spatial information processing.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical overlap with LR dendrites in L1a

claim: Selective ablation of putative retrosplenial RS cells located near the boundary and within upper layer 5 resulted in contextual fear amnesia.
source: Indeed, a recent study reported that selective ablation of putative retrosplenial RS cells located near the boundary and within upper layer 5 resulted in contextual fear amnesia (Sigwald et al., 2020), indicating that these cells are involved in the fear-related functions of the retrosplenial cortex (Lukoyanov and Lukoyanova, 2006; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Both the CLA and ACC have been heavily implicated in fear-associated behaviors.
source: Both the CLA (Cho et al., 2017; Ipser et al., 2013; Vakolyuk et al., 1980; Vetere et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2018) and ACC Frankland et al., 2004; Han et al., 2003; Steenland et al., 2012 have been heavily implicated in fear-associated behaviors, suggesting again that CLA and ACC inputs to L3 RS cells help to support the role of these neurons in contextual fear conditioning.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: CLA and ACC inputs to L3 RS cells help to support the role of these neurons in contextual fear conditioning.
source: Both the CLA (Cho et al., 2017; Ipser et al., 2013; Vakolyuk et al., 1980; Vetere et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2018) and ACC Frankland et al., 2004; Han et al., 2003; Steenland et al., 2012 have been heavily implicated in fear-associated behaviors, suggesting again that CLA and ACC inputs to L3 RS cells help to support the role of these neurons in contextual fear conditioning.
evidence: Inferred from the involvement of CLA and ACC in fear behaviors and their targeting of RS cells
